newsitem.title: USA: Republicans get big cash support from tobacco.
newsitem.headline: Republicans get big cash support from tobacco.

text.p: Insurance and tobacco interests together gave more than $3 million to Republican national party committees in the first six months of 1997, an independent watchdog group reported on Monday.
Common Cause, a non-partisan group that monitors campaign fund-raising, analyzed all contributions of $10,000 or more during the first half of this year.
It found that insurance companies donated almost $1.7 million to the Republicans, more than nine times as much as they contributed in 1993 in the six months following the last presidential election.
The top single contribution of $1 million came from Richard DeVos of Amway Corp. and his wife.
Tobacco companies gave almost $1.6 million to the Republicans, led by Philip Morris Cos. Inc. with $653,000 and RJR Nabisco Inc. and its RJ Reynolds subsidiary with $340,000.
Contributions from tobacco interests ran five times greater than in the corresponding period four years ago.
Labor unions, lawyers and lobbyists led contributors to Democratic national party committees. Unions gave a little less than $1 million while lawyers and lobbyists donated $818,000.
Overall, Republican and Democratic national party committees raised a combined $34.3 million with Republicans outraising Democrats by more than two to one, $23 million to $11 million.

All these contributions were in the form of so-called "soft money" which is supposed to be used for organization and party building activities and cannot be used to support the campaigns of specific candidates.
However, that distinction has become little more than a fiction as both parties have stretched the legal boundaries to their limits, and in some cases beyond.
Under several proposals circulating in Congress, soft money contributions would be banned. However, such legislation is seen as having little chance of becoming law.

The report showed 17 companies gave donations of $50,000 or more to both parties. Common Cause President Ann McBride said that showed the contributions were designed to retain access and influence regardless of which party was in office.
